name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,349

blocks.note: to hare off somewhere is to run at full pelt
m = married, as on a form

annotation.surface: An order to manage the accommodation set aside for the married women.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run' reads as an instruction to manage a place and is the verb for going fast, which is where the first four letters come from. The hare is the crossword's standard runner.
annotation.definitionFit: A harem is the part of a Muslim household reserved for the wives, so it is the women's quarters in the literal sense.

entries.clue: Warm through hearts and have meal ... (4)

blocks.note: h is the card suit's initial, standard shorthand in wordplay
to have a meal is to eat

annotation.surface: Warming the food right through, then sitting down to a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots hand the sentence on to 2 down, so the two clues read as one thought about supper. H for hearts comes off the card table and is worth banking.
annotation.definitionFit: To heat something is to warm it through — the verb a recipe uses for bringing a dish up to temperature.

entries.clue: ... ready to complain where starter missed (4)

indicatorNotes.missed: Something missed is not there at all, so the letter named beside it never reaches the answer.

blocks.note: to gripe is to complain, and grumblingly at that
a word's starter is its first letter, the g here

annotation.surface: A diner ready to grumble because the first course never arrived.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots carry on from 1 down, so 'starter missed' first reads as a course that never came; the setter means the first letter of a word instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Ripe fruit is ready to be picked or eaten, which is the word a grower would use in its place.

entries.clue: Put on speed in Winnebago say (9)

blocks.note: to motor along is to travel fast
'is she home?' asks exactly what 'is she in?' asks

annotation.surface: Picking up speed inside a camper van.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is the word doing the hiding: on the surface it puts the speeding inside the vehicle, and in the wordplay it means at home. Nothing else in the clue instructs anything.
annotation.definitionFit: A Winnebago is one American make of motorhome, so 'say' marks the brand as an example standing in for the whole class.

indicatorNotes.dreadfully: Something in a dreadful state is not as it should be, and letters in that state are not left in the order handed over.

blocks.note: seven letters, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: One deed described as terribly wicked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dreadfully' reads as an intensifier strengthening the wickedness while being the clue's only instruction. Short anagrams hide best in ordinary grammar: 'An act is' looks like the start of a sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Satanic means of or like Satan, so it is evil of the blackest kind rather than mere naughtiness.

indicatorNotes.demolishing: Demolishing something knocks it down, and the letters it acts on come apart and are rebuilt elsewhere.

blocks.note: six letters of plain diary English, taken for their spelling

annotation.surface: A date fixed for knocking a stable down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like the building the demolition is booked for and is the definition, meaning firm and unwavering. That leaves 'Day set' to be the letters, which is hard to see because it reads as a diary entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A steady hand or a steady job is stable — unwavering, in no danger of shifting.

indicatorNotes.covering: To cover something is to lie over it and keep it out of sight, so the word before hides the letters wanted.

blocks.note: three consecutive letters inside the garment, starting at its fourth

annotation.surface: A costume that covers the stomach.
annotation.walkthrough: Three letters need very little hiding room, so the one long word is where to look. Costume and belly belong to the same picture of dressing up, which keeps the seam between definition and wordplay out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Tum is the nursery word for the stomach — the belly as a child, or a doctor talking to one, would name it.

blocks.note: late in the day is night
a jar is a glass of beer in British pub talk — 'fancy a jar?'

annotation.surface: Standing a late drink for a scatterbrained sort.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flighty sort' pretends to mean a frivolous person and means a thing with wings: the nightjar is a bird that hunts moths at dusk. JAR for beer is pub idiom worth banking.
annotation.definitionFit: The nightjar flies by night after insects, so 'flighty' picks it out by its wings while pretending to describe a person's character.

entries.clue: Writer Raymond one with wicked output (8)

blocks.note: the American novelist who invented the detective Philip Marlowe
a maker of candles, and what runs down the middle of a candle is a wick

annotation.surface: A crime novelist whose books are full of villainy.
annotation.walkthrough: Raymond Chandler wrote the Marlowe novels, and a chandler makes candles — so 'wicked' is a pun on wick, not a word about sin. The surface wants the wickedness to be his plots.
annotation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler is the writer of the Marlowe novels; and a chandler's output is candles, every one of them fitted with a wick.

entries.clue: Alpha male turned up with peg — Long John Silver? (7)

indicatorNotes.turned: Something turned is facing the other way, so the little word beside it is written back to front.

blocks.note: a for alpha, first letter of the Greek and of the radio alphabet
m = male, as on a form
the two letters of 'up' written the other way round
the peg a golf ball is balanced on

annotation.surface: The alpha male arrives carrying a peg, like the pirate with the wooden leg.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived and is an instruction to write two letters backwards. Long John Silver is Treasure Island's one-legged pirate, and 'peg' keeps him in view while quietly meaning a golf tee.
annotation.definitionFit: Long John Silver has lost a leg and stumps about on a crutch, so the question mark offers him as one famous instance rather than a synonym.

indicatorNotes.stores: To store something is to keep it inside, so what follows goes within the word before it.

blocks.note: mama is the fuller nursery form of mum
g is the abbreviation for gallons, as on a fuel figure

annotation.surface: Mother keeping gallons of something in store.
annotation.walkthrough: Mum reaches past the two-letter MA a solver expects to the longer MAMA, which is where the room for an insertion comes from. The colon does all the joining, so no link word says which half is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Magma is the molten rock that sits under a volcano and is only called lava once it has come out.

entries.clue: King Edward quit throne, leaving British destroyed (10)

indicatorNotes.leaving: To leave a place is to go from it, so the letter named next departs the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: Edwardus Rex, the Latin signature of an Edward on the throne
to abdicate is to give up a throne
b = British, the standard short form

annotation.surface: A king called Edward gives up his throne and leaves Britain in ruins.
annotation.walkthrough: Edward VIII really did abdicate, in 1936, which is what holds the surface together. ER is the crossword's regnal signature, Rex or Regina behind the initial, and here it is an Edward rather than the usual queen.
annotation.definitionFit: To eradicate something is to pull it up by the roots and leave none of it, so 'destroyed' is the past sense at its most thorough.

entries.clue: Capital he wasted in Islamic empire (9)

indicatorNotes.wasted: A place laid waste is left a heap in which nothing keeps its old position, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: nine letters, taken for their spelling and not their sense

annotation.surface: The money he frittered away inside a Muslim empire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' invites a hunt for a city or a fortune and is only letters. A caliph is Muhammad's successor as ruler of the faithful, which is why the definition can be so plain.
annotation.definitionFit: A caliphate is the territory ruled by a caliph, successor to Muhammad, so it is an Islamic empire in the literal sense.

entries.clue: White female abandoning chips and fish (8)

indicatorNotes.abandoning: To abandon something is to walk out and leave it, so the letter named goes from the word it was in.

blocks.note: chips are fries on the other side of the Atlantic
f = female, as on a form, and it is the letter that walks out
the ling is a long North Atlantic food fish, a relative of the cod

annotation.surface: A white woman walking away from her fish and chips.
annotation.walkthrough: 'White' is a wine and not a person, though the surface keeps it attached to 'female' for as long as it can. Riesling is the German grape a wine list files under that one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Riesling is a white grape and the wine pressed from it, so 'White' is the class a wine list puts it in.

blocks.note: what a crossword is built from, one for every entry
less means fewer, whatever the pedants say about countables
surface only — it makes the sentence about a setter's workload and adds no letters

annotation.surface: A setter told it would be daft to write fewer crosswords.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is at the setter's own expense: put fewer of the things a crossword is made of into one and you are what the answer calls you. The two halves come out in the reverse of the clue's order, with nothing marking the switch.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody clueless has no idea what is going on, which is the everyday way of calling them stupid.

indicatorNotes.Endless: Something endless has no end, so the word beside it gives up its final letter.
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts what stands before it inside what comes after, so the shortened word goes within the island.

blocks.note: Is. is the atlas abbreviation for island
despondency is gloom, here going without its last letter

annotation.surface: Unrelieved misery inside the houses of some island.
annotation.walkthrough: Is. for island comes off maps rather than dictionaries. The definition is the last word alone, so everything before it is wordplay — which is what keeps the seam hidden in a sentence that reads perfectly straight.
annotation.definitionFit: An igloo is a house built of snow blocks and lived in, so 'homes' names them by what they are for.

indicatorNotes.almost: 'almost' stops just short of the whole word, so the last letter of the one beside it is never written.

blocks.note: also means too, stopped one letter short of the end
ace = wonderful, first-rate

annotation.surface: Lorraine's other half is nearly too marvellous for words.
annotation.walkthrough: Alsace-Lorraine is the pair of regions on France's German border, annexed together and fought over for a century, which is what makes 'partner' fair. Lorraine reads as a woman's name for as long as you let it.
annotation.definitionFit: Alsace and Lorraine are the two French border provinces always named as a couple, so each is the other's partner.

entries.clue: Take meaningful look round very fast (6)

indicatorNotes.round: Something going round another thing encloses it, so the letter for very ends up inside the longer word.

blocks.note: to take a long meaningful look at somebody is to stare
v = very, as in 'v. good' on a school report

annotation.surface: Having a hard look at something moving very fast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast' is the last word and the definition, which is exactly where a solver reads it as part of the wordplay instead. V for very comes off school reports and margin notes.
annotation.definitionFit: To starve is to go without food and to fast is to do the same deliberately, so the two verbs meet on the going without.

entries.clue: See poet try ridiculously worn-out image (10)

indicatorNotes.ridiculously: What is done ridiculously is done with no proper sense to it, and letters treated so are not in the order given.

blocks.note: ten letters, wanted for their spelling and not their sense

annotation.surface: Watching a poet make a ludicrous attempt at something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'See' at the front of a clue usually points to another entry in the grid, which is why it is easy to skip past instead of counting it into the letters. The definition is the noun phrase at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A stereotype is a fixed, over-familiar picture of a whole group of people — an image worn out by repetition.

indicatorNotes.periodically: Something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so letters are taken at a fixed step — every second one, and only one of the two runs spells anything.

blocks.note: every second letter of the philosopher's name, counting from the second

annotation.surface: The German philosopher hands you an occasional advantage.
annotation.walkthrough: Heidegger is the German philosopher of Being and Time, and the clue wants nothing of his thought, only the spelling of his name. 'Periodically' is the gentler cousin of 'oddly' and 'evenly'.
annotation.definitionFit: An edge over a rival is an advantage, and a narrow one — the margin that puts you just ahead.

entries.clue: King with no time for Windsor perhaps (4)

blocks.note: k = king, on the chessboard and in a pack of cards
the word itself, taken as it stands
t = time, as in the physicist's formulas

annotation.surface: A monarch who hasn't a moment to spare for Windsor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No time' looks like an instruction to throw out a T and is simply NO and T laid down in order. Windsor is the town and the castle on the surface, and a way of tying a tie in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The Windsor is a broad symmetrical way of tying a necktie, so 'perhaps' offers it as one particular example.

blocks.note: i is the symbol for electric current in every formula from Ohm's law on
a deal is an arrangement struck between two parties

annotation.surface: The arrangement in force at the moment suits everybody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current' means present-day on the surface and electrical in the wordplay. There is no link word at all, the definition simply abutting the wordplay, which is what makes three words read as one flat statement.
annotation.definitionFit: Something ideal could not be bettered, so 'just right' is the idiom you would say in its place.

blocks.note: the French word for 'the', masculine singular
a = advanced, as in the A of A-level

annotation.surface: The French pressing forward across a field.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The French' is the crossword's standing request for the French word for 'the' rather than for a Frenchman. A for advanced comes from the A-level, the exam English schools sit at eighteen.
annotation.definitionFit: A lea is an open stretch of grassland, the poets' and the crossword's word for a meadow.

entries.clue: African managed to keep magical staff (7)

indicatorNotes.to keep: To keep something is to hold on to it, so the word after goes inside the word before.

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it, and this is the past tense
the stick a magician waves

annotation.surface: An African who ran things and held on to a magic wand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' wants to be a workforce, and the word in front turns it into a stick — a conjuror's rather than a manager's. The definition is one word long and stands at the front, where it reads as the sentence's subject.
annotation.definitionFit: A Rwandan is a national of Rwanda in east Africa, so 'African' names the answer by the wider class it falls into.

blocks.note: g = good, as in a mark on a school report
an estate is property — land with whatever stands on it

annotation.surface: A fine piece of land ripe for development.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as an estate agent's line, and building on land is exactly what 'develop' means there. In the answer it is a pregnancy, and the verb belongs to the womb.
annotation.definitionFit: To gestate is to carry young and let them develop before birth, so 'develop' is the verb it comes down to.

indicatorNotes.at last: 'at last' points to the end of the word before it, so only that word's final letter is taken.

blocks.note: the ninth and final letter of the word
a vent is an opening cut to let air through

annotation.surface: A famous person finally cutting the ribbon on a show.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a celebrity at a gala, and 'opening' turns out to be a hole for air. The question mark admits the definition is loose: a show is one kind of event and not the whole of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: An event is anything staged for people to attend, and a show is one kind of it — which is what the question mark concedes.
